messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Firstly, there is no reproducible example to enable those who want to help you to help you.
Secondly, you don't report what happens when you run this (non-reproducible) code. More specifically, what does this mean: "...I'm unable to pass the variables into the function." ???

I did a little surgery on your input data frame to m_ply():

> lolimy <- c(145.3, .691,292 )
> uplimy <- c(367.8, .769, 408)

> nms <- LETTERS[1:3]

> pardf <- data.frame(nms, lolimy, uplimy)

> str(pardf)
'data.frame':   3 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ nms   : Factor w/ 3 levels "A","B","C": 1 2 3
 $ lolimy: num  145.3 0.691 292
 $ uplimy: num  367.8 0.769 408

Notice that nms is a factor. It should probably be character instead. To get that, use
data.frame(nms, lolimy, uplimy, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

> pardf
  nms  lolimy  uplimy
1   A 145.300 367.800
2   B   0.691   0.769
3   C 292.000 408.000

It's entirely possible that nms as a factor is an issue in the function call - perhaps it's expecting a character string for nms rather than a factor level...which brings up the notion of using aes_string() instead of aes() inside the geoms. Consult ?aes_string in ggplot2. Other than that, the variables are in the same order as the arguments of the function, so that part of it should not be a problem. m_ply() will process one line of the input matrix/data frame per iteration, so you should get nrow(pardf) plots when you get the function to work. Having looked over the function, I'm pretty certain the error is within the body of plotfun().

Suggestion: Insert browser() into the first line of your function and step through your function line by line to see what it's actually doing. You have the capacity within browser() to investigate the objects being created as the function proceeds, so you can see what works and what doesn't. See section 4.1 of the Writing R Extensions manual for the basics of using browser() if it's not familiar to you.

plotfun <- function(nms, lolimy, uplimy) {
  print(qplot(DATETIME, nms, data=colormrg, geom="line") +
         geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin=start, xmax=end, fill=onoff) ,
                           ymin=lolimy, ymax=uplimy, data=lights) +

         scale_fill_manual(values=alpha(c("blue","red"),.2))
        )
     }

I'm guessing you're going to need a character string for nms wrapped inside an aes_string() code chunk for qplot(). [I don't use qplot() myself, so check that you can run aes_string() within qplot() first. I know you can in ggplot().] Your function also assumes that DATETIME is a variable in colormrg, and start, end, onoff, lolimy and uplimy are variables in a data frame named lights. Is that the case? Finally, I believe you're not going to be able to assign values in scale_fill_manual() unless you specify the breaks first.

Hope something amid all this speculation is relevant to your problem.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

thanks for all the suggestions! When I tried Baptistes solution with my plots, they came out too narrow, as well. I thus figured that the plots themselves must be the problem and shrunk all opts to a minimum (axis.text.x, axis.text.y, strip.background, etc.). It works now, the final code is this (plots is a list with ggplot2 objects):

> grid.newpage()
> pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(length(plots), 1)))
>

> cols <- sapply(plots, findNumber)

> factors <-  cols / max(cols)
>

> for(i in 1:length(plots)){
>     h <- unit(1, 'npc')
>     w <- factors[i] * unit(1, 'npc')
>     if(i < length(plots)){
>       print(plots[[i]] + opts(legend.position = 'none'),
>             vp = vplayout(i, 1, width = w, height = h))}
>   else {
>     print(plots[[i]], vp = vplayout(i, 1, width = w, height = h))}
> }

Best,
Paul

Not perfectly sure this is what you are after -- only read this quickly -- but have you looked at R package CircStats? The stats it covers involve statistics in a circle (sphere, etc.), e.g. clocks, that don't begin at 0 and end at 24 or 360 or whatever -- they are "smooth" and continuous through what ordinary statistics consider a discontinuity.

Not at all an ace on using them, sorry. But a colleague used them to look at reaction rates in a cylindrical vessel with great results. There's a paper that might (or might not) help: google "Circular Dataimages for Directional Data" by Bill Morphet. (Recommend the color version, if you can track it down.)

messages.subject: Re: custom stat question
messages.subject_clean: custom stat question
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The introductory sentence of section 5.9 of Hadley's ggplot2 book
says: "It's often useful to be able to summarise the y values for each
unique x value. In ggplot2, this role is played by stat_summary()..."

In other words, ggplot2 can handle summaries of a response variable
wrt one (categorical) variable. In your code, the aggregate()
statement generated the mean of the level combinations of two
variables. AFAIK, the ability to summarize over more than one (factor)
variable isn't built into stat_summary().

One can do some very nice things with stat_summary(), but it was not
intended to make ggplot() or qplot() a 'one-stop shop' for general
data summarization and graphics. In your case, the way you did it is
best. The problem is that you're trying to average index by country at
a fixed age, but country isn't represented in the plot, so it would be
difficult for stat_summary() to produce the average. (I won't say
impossible, since someone could come along and say 'not so!', but it
would not be trivial). OTOH, this is a fairly trivial calculation in
ddply(), aggregate() or a half-dozen or so other summary functions
available in R. The other advantage of producing summaries prior to
plotting is that you can check them to see if they make sense.

It's often recommended to do the statistical summaries outside of
ggplot() since the function allows different data frames to be read in
different layers. In this case, you only need the summary data as
input to ggplot(), but in other cases it makes sense to pass the
entire data frame into ggplot() for certain layers of the plot and use
a summary data frame to produce additional layers of interest.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: logic behind behavior of stat_sum with a factor variable in x?
messages.subject_clean: logic behind behavior of stat_sum with a factor variable in x?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

It's the default grouping in ggplot2 - if you don't specify otherwise,
all categorical variables in the plot form grouping variables, and the
default in stat_sum is to show the proportion.  You either want:

ggplot(Contraception,aes(x=use,y=livch))+stat_sum(aes(group = 1))

or

ggplot(Contraception,aes(x=use,y=livch))+stat_sum(aes(size = ..n..))

Jake: we need to describe this better in the stat_sum documentation.

Hadley

On Sep 26, 5:20 am, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> The introductory sentence of section 5.9 of Hadley's ggplot2 book
> says: "It's often useful to be able to summarise the y values for each
> unique x value. In ggplot2, this role is played by stat_summary()..."
>
> In other words, ggplot2 can handle summaries of a response variable
> wrt one (categorical) variable. In your code, the aggregate()
> statement generated the mean of the level combinations of two
> variables. AFAIK, the ability to summarize over more than one (factor)
> variable isn't built into stat_summary().
>
> One can do some very nice things with stat_summary(), but it was not
> intended to make ggplot() or qplot() a 'one-stop shop' for general
> data summarization and graphics. In your case, the way you did it is
> best. The problem is that you're trying to average index by country at
> a fixed age, but country isn't represented in the plot, so it would be
> difficult for stat_summary() to produce the average. (I won't say
> impossible, since someone could come along and say 'not so!', but it
> would not be trivial). OTOH, this is a fairly trivial calculation in
> ddply(), aggregate() or a half-dozen or so other summary functions
> available in R. The other advantage of producing summaries prior to
> plotting is that you can check them to see if they make sense.
>
> It's often recommended to do the statistical summaries outside of
> ggplot() since the function allows different data frames to be read in
> different layers. In this case, you only need the summary data as
> input to ggplot(), but in other cases it makes sense to pass the
> entire data frame into ggplot() for certain layers of the plot and use
> a summary data frame to produce additional layers of interest.
>
> HTH,
> Dennis
>

messages.body_plain:
I can parameterize what variable I want to plot in ggplot by constructing my own 'aes' object, like this:

> data <- data.frame(a=1:10,b=11:20)
> col <- quote(b)   # parameter to below
> ggplot(data) + geom_point( structure(list(x=quote(a), y= col ), class= "uneval"))
>
or
> aese <- function(...) structure(eval(substitute(list(...))), class="uneval")
> ggplot(data) + geom_point( aese(x=quote(a), y= col ))

Is there a cleaner or more standard way to do this?

messages.subject: Re: stat_summary(fun.y=var,geom=c("point","smooth"))
messages.subject_clean: stat_summary(fun.y=var,geom=c("point","smooth"))
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It is common to combine multiple geoms into a single plot, but they
are applied individually in separate layers. If your question is 'can
I apply multiple geoms at once into a single layer?' then the answer
is no. A single geom, on the other hand, allows the use of multiple
aesthetics. The + operator exists to allow one to add additional
layers as needed to a ggplot. Most people who produce relatively
complicated graphics in ggplot2 eventually move to using ggplot()
rather than qplot(), but it is certainly possible to add layers to
qplot() as well using the + operator.

Here's a plot I did tonight using some baseball data; the data are not
included, but the plot code illustrates the point:

ggplot(topHitters, aes(x = yearID, y = BA)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = ba400), size = 2.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.400, size = 1) +
    geom_text(data = bignames, aes(x = yearID + xoffset, y = BA + yoffset,
                                   label = nameLast), size = 3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c('FALSE' = 'black', 'TRUE' = 'red')) +
    ylim(0.330, 0.430) +
    xlab('Year') +
    scale_y_continuous('Batting average',
                       breaks = seq(0.34, 0.42, by = 0.02),
                       labels = c('.340', '.360', '.380', '.400', '.420')) +
    geom_smooth() +
    opts(legend.position = 'none')

This plot contains points in a scatterplot, a horizontal reference
line, some text labels, separate colors for the points above and below
the reference line (indicated by a factor ba400 created in the data)
plus a means of assigning colors with the scale_manual() construct. I
then restrict the range of the y-axis, label the x-axis, fix labels
for the y-axis so that I get three decimal places rather than the
default two, add a loess curve to illustrate the trend over time and
finally, get rid of the legend. The plot is meant to resemble one that
appeared in the New York Times the Sunday before last (the loess curve
is graphical sugar :). There are five layers, three scale adjustments
and one line of code to remove the legend. Note that items within an
aes() statement are variables, while those outside aes() are set to a
constant value.

If this is new to you, the arguments to ggplot() are firstly, the data
frame, and secondly, the primary aesthetics that are intended to
persist in all layers of the plot (here, year and average, the x and y
variables). Notice that in geom_text(), another data frame was used,
containing labels and positional offsets to avoid overlapping of
labels in the final plot.

If you want to create 'template' plots for certain applications, you
can always write a function (or collection of functions) to produce
them; that's one way to approach what you seem to have in mind.
Another option, if you're more inclined toward interactive
construction of plots, is to look into the Deducer package, which is,
roughly speaking, a type of GUI for R with support for ggplot2 that
gives you the ability to create your own geoms from existing ones. It
uses the JGR package, which in turn requires the rJava package as its
engine. See the Deducer package home page for more details if you're
interested.
http://www.deducer.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php?n=Main.DeducerManual

Hope this is at least close to answering your question...
Dennis

facet_grid(x~y, labeller="label_both") produces:

x: x1 |  x: x2 | x: x3

and

y: y1 | y: y2 | y:y3

messages.body_plain:
In the following code, the first call to ggtestPlot works, but the
second call to the function produces and error message. The layer
function appears to be trying to access the global variable instead of
the local variable.
...
> dev.new <http://dev.new>()
> rm(xvals);rm(yvals)
> ggtestPlot(rnorm(50))
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'xvals' not found

the code also runs successfully if I replace the lines in the function
with

	xvals <<- seq(0,1,.1)
	yvals <<- seq(1,0,-.1)

=================

ggtestPlot <- function(x)
{
	library(ggplot2)

	xvals <- seq(0,1,.1)
	yvals <- seq(1,0,-.1)

	print(ggplot(data.frame(x), aes(x=x)) +
	geom_histogram(binwidth = .05, fill="light blue") +
	layer(mapping  =  aes(x  =  xvals,  y  =  yvals), geom  =  "line",
stat  =  "identity") )
}

yvals <- xvals <- seq(.9,.1,-.1)
ggtestPlot(rnorm(50))
dev.new <http://dev.new>()
rm(xvals);rm(yvals)
ggtestPlot(rnorm(50))

On Sep 27, 4:17 am, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> It is common to combine multiple geoms into a single plot, but they
> are applied individually in separate layers. If your question is 'can
> I apply multiple geoms at once into a single layer?' then the answer
> is no. A single geom, on the other hand, allows the use of multiple
> aesthetics. The + operator exists to allow one to add additional
> layers as needed to a ggplot. Most people who produce relatively
> complicated graphics in ggplot2 eventually move to using ggplot()
> rather than qplot(), but it is certainly possible to add layers to
> qplot() as well using the + operator.
>
> Here's a plot I did tonight using some baseball data; the data are not
> included, but the plot code illustrates the point:
>
> ggplot(topHitters, aes(x = yearID, y = BA)) +
>     geom_point(aes(colour = ba400), size = 2.5) +
>     geom_hline(yintercept = 0.400, size = 1) +
>     geom_text(data = bignames, aes(x = yearID + xoffset, y = BA + yoffset,
>                                    label = nameLast), size = 3) +
>     scale_colour_manual(values = c('FALSE' = 'black', 'TRUE' = 'red')) +
>     ylim(0.330, 0.430) +
>     xlab('Year') +
>     scale_y_continuous('Batting average',
>                        breaks = seq(0.34, 0.42, by = 0.02),
>                        labels = c('.340', '.360', '.380', '.400', '.420')) +
>     geom_smooth() +
>     opts(legend.position = 'none')
>
> This plot contains points in a scatterplot, a horizontal reference
> line, some text labels, separate colors for the points above and below
> the reference line (indicated by a factor ba400 created in the data)
> plus a means of assigning colors with the scale_manual() construct. I
> then restrict the range of the y-axis, label the x-axis, fix labels
> for the y-axis so that I get three decimal places rather than the
> default two, add a loess curve to illustrate the trend over time and
> finally, get rid of the legend. The plot is meant to resemble one that
> appeared in the New York Times the Sunday before last (the loess curve
> is graphical sugar :). There are five layers, three scale adjustments
> and one line of code to remove the legend. Note that items within an
> aes() statement are variables, while those outside aes() are set to a
> constant value.
>
> If this is new to you, the arguments to ggplot() are firstly, the data
> frame, and secondly, the primary aesthetics that are intended to
> persist in all layers of the plot (here, year and average, the x and y
> variables). Notice that in geom_text(), another data frame was used,
> containing labels and positional offsets to avoid overlapping of
> labels in the final plot.
>
> If you want to create 'template' plots for certain applications, you
> can always write a function (or collection of functions) to produce
> them; that's one way to approach what you seem to have in mind.
> Another option, if you're more inclined toward interactive
> construction of plots, is to look into the Deducer package, which is,
> roughly speaking, a type of GUI for R with support for ggplot2 that
> gives you the ability to create your own geoms from existing ones. It
> uses the JGR package, which in turn requires the rJava package as its
> engine. See the Deducer package home page for more details if you're

> interested.http://www.deducer.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php?n=Main.DeducerManual

>
> Hope this is at least close to answering your question...
> Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I don't know what 'works' means to you, but there are several ways one
can interpret your code. Here are a few attempts that 'work', but
yield different outcomes:

# Use geom_abline():

d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(50))
testPlot <- function(df) {
    print(ggplot(df, aes(x = x)) +
        geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
        geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = -1, size = 1)  )
    }
testPlot(d)

This has the effect of fitting a line of slope -1 throughout the
plotting region. If you want the line's extent to be restricted to the
unit square, then you can create a data frame of coordinates and pass
that in as the data in the layer that produces the line, as Hadley
suggested:

d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(50))
coords <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 1, 0.1), y = seq(1, 0, -0.1))
# coords <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = (1, 0))    ## gets the same line

ggplot() +
   geom_histogram(data = d, aes(x = x), binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
   geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

If you prefer a density histogram over a frequency histogram, then use

ggplot() +
   geom_histogram(data = d, aes(x = x, y = ..density..),
                                   binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
   geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

Sometimes it's necessary to resort to <<- , but it shouldn't be used
unless you know what you're doing (and even then, you should usually
rethink why you're using it). You resort to this ploy because x and y
are not 'visible' to ggplot() inside the print() command of your
function unless they exist in the global environment, which
demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding on your part of how data
are passed in ggplot(). Firstly, it expects data frames. Always. This
is well documented. Secondly, you can import multiple data frames with
different data in different layers. This is one of the features that
gives ggplot() more power and flexibility. The code above illustrates
the idea: the ggplot() call has an empty default data frame, which
requires each layer to have its own data = argument. In this case, the
data frame d is used to generate the histogram while the data frame
coords is used to generate the line.

One can also have a default data frame and pass a new data frame into
a specific layer; the following addition of geom_rug() is a little
silly in this context, but the point is that a geom will look for its
input data from the default data frame unless told otherwise by
specification of data = within a geom statement:

ggplot(d) +
   geom_histogram(aes(x = x, y = ..density..),
                                   binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
   geom_rug(aes(x = x)) +
   geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

ggplot() defines the defaults for each layer in the plot: more
specifically, the default data frame and default aesthetics that are
expected to be present in all successive layers. In this example, x is
a common aesthetic (although it doesn't have the same values in the
line geom) but y is not, so we could shorten the code a bit by making
x a default aesthetic, but not y:

ggplot(d, aes(x = x)) +
   geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..),
                                   binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
   geom_rug() +
   geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

Since x is to be redefined in the geom_line() layer, it needs to be
stated as an aesthetic in reference to the coords data frame. Try it
without x and see what happens.

To wrap all this inside a function,

testPlot2 <- function(df1, df2) {
   print(
      ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = x)) +
           geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..),
                           binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
           geom_rug() +
           geom_line(data = df2, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)
        )
   }
testPlot2(d, coords)

It also occurred to me that you could use geom_segment() to produce
the line just as easily, thus dispensing with the coords data frame
altogether:

ggplot(d) +
   geom_histogram(aes(x = x, y = ..density..),
                               binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
   geom_segment(aes(x = 0), xend = 1, y = 1, yend = 0)

Even though x is not variable within geom_segment(), it needs to be
wrapped in aes() because it is not the same x as that in the default
data frame d, which geom_segment() is reading by default. In fact, I
found four ways to get geom_segment() to produce the same line: two
using aes() and two with external one line data frames. The second
aes() statement I used was

geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = 1, yend = 0), legend = FALSE)

Take out the legend = FALSE line, see what happens and ask yourself
why that occurred.

HTH,
Dennis

Hi:

I don't know what 'works' means to you, but there are several ways one
can interpret your code. Here are a few attempts that 'work', but
yield different outcomes:

# Use geom_abline():

d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(50))
testPlot <- function(df) {
    print(ggplot(df, aes(x = x)) +
        geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
        geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = -1, size = 1)  )
    }
testPlot(d)

This has the effect of fitting a line of slope -1 throughout the
plotting region. If you want the line's extent to be restricted to the
unit square, then you can create a data frame of coordinates and pass
that in as the data in the layer that produces the line, as Hadley
suggested:

d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(50))
coords <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 1, 0.1), y = seq(1, 0, -0.1))
# coords <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = (1, 0))    ## gets the same line

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(data = d, aes(x = x), binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
  geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

If you prefer a density histogram over a frequency histogram, then use

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(data = d, aes(x = x, y = ..density..),
                                  binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
  geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

Sometimes it's necessary to resort to <<- , but it shouldn't be used
unless you know what you're doing (and even then, you should usually
rethink why you're using it). You resort to this ploy because x and y
are not 'visible' to ggplot() inside the print() command of your
function unless they exist in the global environment, which
demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding on your part of how data
are passed in ggplot(). Firstly, it expects data frames. Always. This
is well documented. Secondly, you can import multiple data frames with
different data in different layers. This is one of the features that
gives ggplot() more power and flexibility. The code above illustrates
the idea: the ggplot() call has an empty default data frame, which
requires each layer to have its own data = argument. In this case, the
data frame d is used to generate the histogram while the data frame
coords is used to generate the line.

One can also have a default data frame and pass a new data frame into
a specific layer; the following addition of geom_rug() is a little
silly in this context, but the point is that a geom will look for its
input data from the default data frame unless told otherwise by
specification of data = within a geom statement:

ggplot(d) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = x, y = ..density..),
                                  binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

ggplot() defines the defaults for each layer in the plot: more
specifically, the default data frame and default aesthetics that are
expected to be present in all successive layers. In this example, x is
a common aesthetic (although it doesn't have the same values in the
line geom) but y is not, so we could shorten the code a bit by making
x a default aesthetic, but not y:

ggplot(d, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..),
                                  binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
  geom_rug() +
  geom_line(data = coords, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)

Since x is to be redefined in the geom_line() layer, it needs to be
stated as an aesthetic in reference to the coords data frame. Try it
without x and see what happens.

To wrap all this inside a function,

testPlot2 <- function(df1, df2) {
  print(
      ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = x)) +
          geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..),
                          binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
          geom_rug() +
          geom_line(data = df2, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 1)
        )
  }
testPlot2(d, coords)

It also occurred to me that you could use geom_segment() to produce
the line just as easily, thus dispensing with the coords data frame
altogether:

ggplot(d) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = x, y = ..density..),
                              binwidth = 0.05, fill = 'lightblue') +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0), xend = 1, y = 1, yend = 0)

Even though x is not variable within geom_segment(), it needs to be
wrapped in aes() because it is not the same x as that in the default
data frame d, which geom_segment() is reading by default. In fact, I
found four ways to get geom_segment() to produce the same line: two
using aes() and two with external one line data frames. The second
aes() statement I used was

geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = 1, yend = 0), legend = FALSE)

Take out the legend = FALSE line, see what happens and ask yourself
why that occurred.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: order x in geom_bar
messages.subject_clean: order x in geom_bar
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

vecx <- c("lmP",  "lmN",  "Nt",   "expG", "expD", "prbN", "prbP")
vecy <- c(43, 20, 1,  6,  0, 19, 10)

d <- data.frame(lab = factor(vecx, levels = vecx), perc = vecy)
ggplot(d, aes(lab, perc)) + geom_bar(stat = 'identity')

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:

relative positioning rather than absolute. That is, I want a position
of (0.5, 0.5) to be dead center regardless of the x and y axis limits.
Is that possible?

Alternatively I could of course transform a relative position to an
absolute one if I had the x and y limits. Is it possible to extract
those from a plot?
